findings.source_passage: There Leviathan, Hugest of living creatures, in the deep Stretched like a promontory sleeps or swims, And seems a moving land; and at his gills Draws in, and at his breath spouts out a sea.
findings.source_locator: Second Paradise Lost extract, after 'That sea beast Leviathan' extract
findings.why_it_matters: This is the more famous and interpretively loaded of the two Paradise Lost extracts—'seems a moving land' is a critical touchstone for the novel's sublime-whale imagery and is widely quoted in Melville scholarship; its absence while the lesser extract is retained is a clear signature failure.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore verbatim: '—"There Leviathan, Hugest of living creatures, in the deep Stretched like a promontory sleeps or swims, And seems a moving land; and at his gills Draws in, and at his breath spouts out a sea." —_Ibid_.' immediately after the first Paradise Lost extract.

findings.source_passage: Mad with the agonies he endures from these fresh attacks, the infuriated Sperm Whale rolls over and over; he rears his enormous head, and with wide expanded jaws snaps at everything around him
findings.source_locator: Thomas Beale's History of the Sperm Whale extract, near end of source
findings.why_it_matters: The Beale extract is the longest single quotation in EXTRACTS and is critically significant—it directly establishes the neglected scientific study of the sperm whale that Melville's cetological chapters implicitly answer; its absence removes a primary interpretive keystone for the whole book's project.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full Beale extract verbatim, including both the action description and the lament about the animal being 'so entirely neglected' by observers—this is too thematically load-bearing to cut.

findings.source_passage: Spain—a great whale stranded on the shores of Europe.
findings.source_locator: Edmund Burke (somewhere) extract, after the Parliament/Nantucket Burke extract
findings.why_it_matters: This is one of the most culturally famous individual lines in the entire EXTRACTS section—Burke's epigram is widely anthologized independently of Moby-Dick and its compression of geopolitical metaphor into whale-imagery is a signature moment; the draft keeps the less famous Burke quotation but drops the more famous one.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore: '"Spain—a great whale stranded on the shores of Europe." —_Edmund Burke_. (_somewhere_.)' immediately after the Parliament Burke extract.

findings.source_passage: Let us fly, let us fly! Old Nick take me if it is not Leviathan described by the noble prophet Moses in the life of patient Job.
findings.why_it_matters: The Rabelais extract is tonally distinctive and famous—its comic panic voice is unlike any other entry in the list and contributes to the tonal range that makes EXTRACTS itself a literary performance rather than a dry bibliography.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore: '"Let us fly, let us fly! Old Nick take me if it is not Leviathan described by the noble prophet Moses in the life of patient Job." —_Rabelais_.' in its original position.

findings.source_passage: The Cachalot (Sperm Whale) is not only better armed than the True Whale (Greenland or Right Whale) in possessing a formidable weapon at either extremity of its body, but also more frequently displays a disposition to employ these weapons offensively
findings.source_locator: Frederick Debell Bennett's Whaling Voyage extract, after Beale extract
findings.why_it_matters: The Bennett extract establishes the sperm whale as uniquely dangerous—a claim that underpins the entire novel's premise; its presence alongside Beale creates the authoritative scientific framing for Moby Dick's threat, and cutting both Beale and Bennett together removes this framing entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the Bennett extract verbatim after the Beale extract; at minimum include the characterization of the Cachalot as 'the most dangerous to attack of all the known species of the whale tribe.'

findings.source_passage: What spermacetti is, men might justly doubt, since the learned Hosmannus in his work of thirty years, saith plainly, Nescio quid sit.
findings.source_locator: Sir T. Browne extract, after Davenant extract
findings.why_it_matters: Sir Thomas Browne is a known stylistic influence on Melville and this extract's learned irony—thirty years of study yielding 'I don't know what it is'—is a voice-signature moment; it also thematically prefigures the novel's epistemological uncertainty about the whale.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the Sir T. Browne extract verbatim, preserving the Latin tag 'Nescio quid sit' which is essential to its ironic force.

findings.source_passage: And what thing soever besides cometh within the chaos of this monster's mouth, be it beast, boat, or stone, down it goes all incontinently that foul great swallow of his, and perisheth in the bottomless gulf of his paunch.
findings.source_locator: Holland's Plutarch's Morals extract, after Tooke's Lucian extract
findings.why_it_matters: This is one of the most rhetorically distinctive lines in the early portion of EXTRACTS—'the bottomless gulf of his paunch' and the tricolon 'beast, boat, or stone' give it a Rabelaisian energy that establishes the monster's all-consuming nature central to the novel's symbolic architecture.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the Holland's Plutarch extract verbatim in its original position after the early scriptural extracts.

findings.source_passage: Io! Paean! Io! sing. To the finny people's king. Not a mightier whale than this In the vast Atlantic is; Not a fatter fish than he, Flounders round the Polar Sea.
findings.source_locator: Charles Lamb's Triumph of the Whale extract
findings.why_it_matters: Charles Lamb's mock-heroic whale poem is one of the few comic-celebratory entries in EXTRACTS and its inclusion by Melville is a deliberate tonal choice; the 'Io! Paean!' opening is immediately recognizable and its loss flattens the emotional register of the compilation.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the Lamb extract verbatim; it is short enough to fit within any reasonable compression budget.

summary: The draft retains roughly 40% of the source extracts and omits multiple high- and medium-priority signatures including the second (more famous) Paradise Lost extract, the thematically critical Beale passage, Burke's 'Spain' epigram, and several voice-distinctive entries (Rabelais, Lamb, Sir T. Browne) that together constitute the literary and interpretive character of the EXTRACTS section.
